title: Helio Bio - Dedicated Capacity & Isolation Intake
summary: Discovery for dedicated GPU reservation, isolation requirements, burst strategy, and scaling expectations for Helio Bio's inference workloads. Customer has strict data residency and compliance constraints; leaning toward a Private/Dedicated hybrid. Key asks: predictable latency at 99th pctl, SOC2 audit artifacts, KMS integration, and a burst/failover playbook. Agreed next steps: share pricing tiers, SOC2 + VPC docs, and coordinate a pilot for 2 weeks of benchmarking.
action_items: Samir - Send Dedicated pricing tiers + commitment options by 2027-01-04
Priya - Share SOC2 + VPC architecture doc and KMS integration notes by 2026-12-30
Liam - Provide 3 weeks of token throughput traces and peak concurrency numbers by 2026-12-31
next_steps: Redwood to send pricing and compliance docs
Schedule a 2-week pilot benchmark in Redwood Dedicated private tenancy (date TBC)
Follow-up call with infra team and CISO to review network/VPC configs
transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-12-28
Start: 14:00 UTC
Duration: 57 minutes
Attendees: Samir Gupta (Redwood AE), Priya Nair (Redwood SE), Maya Chen (Helio Head of ML), Liam O'Connor (Helio Platform), Nora Saleh (Helio CISO)

[00:00] Samir (Redwood AE): Hey everyone, thanks for carving out time. Um, this is Samir from Redwood, AE. With me is Priya, she's our systems engineer. Quick intro from your side?
[00:18] Maya (Helio): Hi, Maya here. Head of ML at Helio Bio. We're looking to move inference off a mix of in-house GPUs and a small hosted vendor, trying to standardize.
[00:25] Liam (Helio): Liam, I run platform. We manage the clusters and scheduling.
[00:30] Nora (Helio): Nora, CISO. I'll be listening for compliance and key management stuff.
[00:35] Samir: Great, thank you. Agenda for today: sizing reserved capacity, isolation and tenancy constraints, burst and prewarm requirements, and what a pilot would look like. Sound good?
[00:44] Maya: Yes. Also, some cost guardrails and latency SLOs.
[00:47] Priya (Redwood SE): Awesome. Quick clarifying question — are you leaning hosted, dedicated, or private deployment? Or hybrid?
[00:55] Maya: We're leaning dedicated/private hybrid. Customer data is PHI-adjacent, so we need strong controls. But we also want the flexibility to fall back to hosted for burst traffic if there's an emergency.
[01:05] Nora: To clarify, PHI adjacent — we need audit logs, KMS, and we need the ability to prove encryption at rest. So SOC2 is a baseline, but we also need controls around key management and tenant isolation.
[01:18] Samir: Understood. Redwood Dedicated can be provisioned inside a VPC with customer-managed networking and KMS integrations; we have options for customer keys or Redwood-managed keys. Priya, do you want to cover how isolation works?
[01:30] Priya: Sure. So in Dedicated we offer reserved GPU pools that are tenant-fenced. That means compute nodes are dedicated to your tenancy; we can enforce node labeling and runtime sandboxing. There's also a warm-pool prewarm to reduce cold start latency. Note: sometimes our transcripts call it Red wood or Red wood ded — sorry, that was a note earlier, but the product is Redwood Dedicated.
[01:51] Liam: Quick question on warm-pool — during big scientific job bursts we see 5–10x baseline qps for short windows, 5–15 minutes. Will the warm pool handle that without preempting other tenants?
[02:05] Priya: If you reserve capacity sized to cover base plus expected burst, warm pools help. For short spikes we recommend a combination of: reserved buffer capacity, a prewarmed hot-pool that you own, and automated fallback to a hosted-compatible model variant. The fallback incurs higher cost but it's quick.
[02:23] Maya: We worry about model parity when falling back — e.g., if you run a quantized variant in hosted fallback it could change output slightly. We have downstream validation that could be affected.
[02:34] Priya: That's a good point. We support model pinning so you can pin a specific binary and quantization profile. But for fallback we may route to a slightly different variant depending on availability. We can add regression checks in your routing policy to prefer quality over cost.
[02:49] Nora: So, on keys — can Helio bring its own KMS? We can't have Redwood hold our keys for anything marked sensitive.
[02:56] Samir: Yes, we integrate with customer KMS providers; you can bring keys and we support external key eviction, HSM-backed KMS workflows. We'll share the doc.
[03:06] [crosstalk] Liam: And audit logs — retention? We need 2 years of audit for certain workflows.
[03:11] Priya: We have configurable retention for request/response logs and trace-level audit logs. Default is 90 days, but enterprise plans can extend to multi-year with additional storage. There are also redaction and policy filters so you don't store raw output unless you opt in.
[03:28] Maya: That's important. We cannot retain raw PHI outputs unless it's encrypted and access-controlled.
[03:34] Priya: Right, we can do token-level redaction and also sentinel-based scrubbing.
[03:40] [00:04:00] Samir: Let's talk about sizing. What does a typical inference request look like for you — average tokens, peak tokens per second, and concurrency?
[04:10] Maya: Our most common inference path is a 512–1,024 token context with a 200–400 token generation. Baseline is about 15 qps, peaks hit 200 qps during batch runs. Concurrency tops at about 120 concurrent requests during the busiest windows.
[04:28] Liam: To add, the token distribution is spiky — long contexts during batch analysis, short context for UI-driven clinician queries.
[04:36] Priya: Ok, that distribution suggests GPU types where memory for KV cache matters. We usually recommend A100 or H100 class instances for your largest models. Are you using open models or private fine-tuned weights?
[04:48] Maya: Both. We have some in-house fine-tuned models for clinical note summarization, and we also evaluate community models. The private weights are the ones that must stay in Helio's tenancy.
[04:58] Samir: For private weights we can host them inside your dedicated private deployment so they never leave your VPC. For hybrid bursts that route to hosted, we'd only route to public model variants unless you enable secure replication — which is possible but requires controls.
[05:12] Nora: How does secure replication work? We need to ensure private models are not copied to shared infrastructure.
[05:18] Priya: Secure replication is optional. It uses encrypted image pulls into pre-provisioned private nodes, with keys managed by you. We ensure no snapshotting to shared pools, and ephemeral caches are cleared on preemption. That said, fallback to hosted would not have access to private models unless you explicitly enable cross-tenancy replication with strict controls.
[05:36] Maya: Good. Next: SLAs. We need 99th percentile latency under 350ms for our clinical UI queries and availability at 99.95. Is that achievable?
[05:47] Samir: For dedicated pools with proper sizing and warm-pool, 99th pctl under 350ms is achievable for many model sizes — depends on sequence length and model family. We can commit to target SLOs in a reserved capacity contract, and monitor closely in Redwood Console.
[05:59] Priya: Important caveat: for very large models with long contexts it may still be challenging to hit 350ms p99; you'd need more GPUs per shard and higher memory. We can run benchmarks in the pilot to validate.
[06:12] [00:07:00] Liam: On the operational side, what does autoscaling look like for Dedicated — can we set policies or is it Redwood-managed?
[06:19] Priya: You can set autoscaling policies: min/max reserved nodes, scale based on queue length or token throughput, and you can set burst thresholds. There's also a policy engine for automatic fallback to hosted models if utilization exceeds a threshold.
[06:33] Liam: And is prewarm billed?
[06:36] Samir: Prewarm capacity is billed in reserved plans; warm-pool usage within your reserved allocation is included, but if you request on-demand burst beyond your commit, that's billed at on-demand rates. We'll include clear unit economics in the pricing sheet.
[06:48] Maya: We need cost modeling — we can't blindly buy double capacity for rare bursts. Can Redwood do dynamic budgeting — like temporary bursts charged to a separate budget bucket?
[06:57] Samir: Yes, you can set burst budgets and alarms. Also, Redwood Optimize can suggest quantization and batching changes to reduce cost while preserving accuracy. But quantization can change outputs slightly.
[07:09] Maya: We saw earlier that quantization reduced hallucination in some models but changed phrasing, which matters for our compliance checks.
[07:16] Priya: We recommend establishing acceptance tests and regression suites — Redwood Console can run evals on canary traffic to check for regressions before promoting a quantized variant.
[07:26] [00:08:00] Nora: Security question — SSO. We require SAML + SCIM provisioning and role-based access control. Can Redwood integrate?
[07:33] Samir: Yes, enterprise plans include SAML SSO, SCIM provisioning, and fine-grained RBAC. We'll share the SSO integration guide.
[07:41] Nora: Also, we need signed audit trails for model invocations and admin actions.
[07:45] Priya: Audit trails are available; we can produce signed logs and provide a separate retention archive for compliance review.
[07:53] Maya: Good. Are there any hard limits around concurrent KV cache size or per-tenant memory?
[07:59] Priya: Limits depend on instance types. For KV cache heavy workloads we choose instance classes with higher GPU memory and we can tune KV sharding. In practice we've seen we can support large cache sizes but it impacts shard count and latency. We'll map your token distribution to a recommended instance and shard layout in the pilot report.
[08:17] Liam: We also need to understand failure modes. If a node fails during a long-running request, what's the retry behavior and what does the client see?
[08:25] Priya: The runtime has transparent retries for short network blips; for in-flight token generation retries are harder because of stateful KV cache. We checkpoint KV state and can rehydrate, but large replays can add latency. For critical UI paths we recommend shorter contexts or pinned prewarmed sessions.
[08:41] Maya: Ok. Can we run a tabletop for failover? Like, simulate pod loss and see service behavior.
[08:46] Samir: Absolutely — included in the pilot as a scenario. We'll coordinate a chaos test with your infra team.
[08:51] [00:09:00] Nora: Legal/procurement note — we have a standard DPA with data residency clauses and want a right-to-audit clause. Is that standard?
[09:00] Samir: We have an enterprise contract template with DPA, data residency options, and audit clauses. We'll share it with your legal.
[09:06] Maya: For the pilot — what's a recommended scope? We want to validate latency and cost for our two main models and test prewarm + fallback during a synthetic burst.
[09:16] Priya: Recommended pilot: 2 weeks, include: 1) baseline benchmark on your models in a dedicated private tenancy; 2) burst test with synthetic 5–10x traffic; 3) failover test to hosted variant; 4) compliance checklist for KMS and audit logs. We'll instrument and deliver a pilot report.
[09:32] Liam: What about telemetry access? Do we get direct Prometheus metrics or only via Redwood Console?
[09:38] Priya: You get both. There's an API for metrics and traces, and we can stream to your metrics backend or provide Prometheus endpoints. Some metrics are sanitized in hosted fallback for privacy reasons.
[09:50] Maya: Sounds good. Pricing — can you sketch options?
[09:54] Samir: High level: reserved capacity is monthly commit by GPU type; dedicated private tenancy has a platform fee + per-GPU rate. Burst overages charged at on-demand per-GPU minute. We also offer committed discounts for annual terms. I'll send the pricing sheet with numbers.
[10:07] Nora: For compliance we may prefer annual commitment if it gives better audit support.
[10:12] Samir: Understood. We'll show a monthly vs annual comparison.
[10:16] [00:11:00] Priya: One more operational detail — image and model lifecycle. How do you want to handle model updates?
[10:22] Maya: Ideally, model updates should go through a canary and A/B rollout with automatic rollback on regressions. We have a validation suite to detect quality regression.
[10:30] Priya: Redwood supports canary/A-B rollouts and automated quality gating — you can plug in your eval suite. We'll capture prompt sets and alignments in the console.
[10:39] Maya: Great. We're also curious about cold-start numbers — when you scale from zero what's the latency?
[10:45] Priya: Cold-start depends on model size. Small models can warm in seconds if prewarmed images are present; large larget models may need tens of seconds to load weights. Warm pools mitigate that.
[10:56] Samir: For the pilot we can instrument cold-start and provide guidance on pool sizing to meet your 350ms p99 goal for UI requests.
[11:06] [00:12:00] Maya: Can you explain the fallback routing granularity — can we route only a percentage of requests to hosted fallback so we don't risk full quality divergence?
[11:15] Priya: Yes, routing policies support percent-based rollouts, latency-based fallbacks, and cost caps. You can set a policy like: 10% of requests route to hosted fallback during normal ops for shadow testing, 100% during emergencies.
[11:29] Liam: Do you support traffic shadowing for unseen changes?
[11:33] Priya: Shadowing is supported — you can shadow to hosted or dedicated variants and run evaluation without impacting production responses.
[11:40] Maya: Perfect. A few more nitty-gritty items: does Redwood keep model provenance logs? We need to know which binary/version answered a request.
[11:48] Priya: Yes, request metadata includes model id, variant id, model checksum, and environment id. That gets stored in the audit trail.
[11:55] Nora: Ok. Final question from me — can we restrict admin operations by IP range and require MFA for admins?
[12:02] Samir: Yes: IP restrictions, SAML-enforced MFA, and role separation are supported. We'll provide a checklist.
[12:09] [00:13:00] Maya: This is all helpful. To move forward we need: 1) pricing and contract template; 2) SOC2 and KMS integration docs; 3) list of GPU types with per-GPU token throughput baselines; 4) pilot schedule.
[12:21] Samir: We'll deliver those. Priya, take the lead on SOC2 and technical docs.
[12:25] Priya: Yep, I'll assemble a pilot runbook and compliance pack.
[12:28] Liam: I'll send the telemetry traces and peak window logs.
[12:31] Nora: Legal will follow up once we get the contract template.
[12:35] Samir: Great. Any blockers we should know about?
[12:38] Maya: Not blockers, but timeline — we want pilot to start mid-Jan if everything looks good.
[12:42] Samir: That works. We'll target mid-Jan start, pending pricing and legal.
[12:46] [00:14:00] Priya: One more note — we occasionally see transcription engines mislabeling KV cache as K-V cash. In case you see docs with that typo, it's the same thing.
[12:55] [laughter] Maya: Noted.
[12:58] Samir: Ok I'll recap next steps now.
[13:02] Samir (recap): Action items: Samir send pricing and contract; Priya share SOC2+KMS+VPC runbook and pilot runbook; Liam provide telemetry traces; Redwood to propose pilot dates mid-Jan. We'll also include a proposed warm-pool sizing and estimated cost for covering 2x baseline with 5–10 minute bursts.
[13:20] Nora: Sounds good.
[13:22] Maya: Thanks everyone. Looking forward to the docs.
[13:26] Samir: Thanks all. We'll follow up via email and create a calendar invite for the pilot kickoff.
[13:32] [end of meeting]

Notes on transcript quality: occasional mis-hearings (quan-tization, K-V cash), speaker overlaps, and some punctuation missing — overall medium quality.
